advances: The continuous affine-average bridge holds for every compact convex support, with an absolute constant. An exponential epigraph using one additional continuous coordinate gives the same scale for every log-concave probability density. Consequently, sufficiently fine complete-lattice approximations of each fixed compact log-affine law satisfy this scale as well. These are continuous and approximation statements, not a solution of the locked mixed-integer conjecture. The projective change of variables does not preserve the integer grid or its atomic weights, and the continuous variance input fails on coarse complete lattices, as the exact calibration at the end of the proof demonstrates.
author: research-agent
external_sources: Matthieu Fradelizi, Mokshay Madiman and Liyao Wang, *Optimal Concentration of Information Content for Log-Concave Densities*, arXiv:1508.04093v2, 26 October 2015, [Theorem 2.3 on page 4, with Definitions 2.1 and 2.2 on pages 3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.04093v2). The exact mathematical assertion used is: if \(X\) is a random vector in \(\mathbb R^k\) with a log-concave probability density \(f\), then \(\operatorname{Var}[-\log f(X)]\leq k\). Their definition permits \(f=e^{-U}\) with convex \(U:\mathbb R^k\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For our compact log-affine law, \(U=\ell+\log Z+I_K\), where \(I_K\) is zero on \(K\) and \(+\infty\) outside, is convex. Almost surely, \(-\log f(X)=\ell(X)+\log Z\), so the theorem gives precisely the variance inequality used above. This is an external analytic theorem, not an accepted project fact or a computational certificate premise.
proof:
The depths integrated below are measurable. Indeed, for an absolutely continuous probability measure, a halfspace can be moved parallel to itself until its boundary contains the specified point, without increasing its mass. For each unit normal \(v\), the mass of \(\{z:v\cdot z\geq v\cdot x\}\) is continuous in \(x\), since hyperplanes have measure zero. The infimum of these continuous functions is upper semicontinuous, hence Borel measurable. Also \(0\leq\tau_\sigma\leq 1\).

We use the uniform-body comparison proved in accepted fact \(7a3ce13723086670\): if \(Q\subset\mathbb R^k\) is a convex body and \(\nu_Q\) is its uniform probability measure, then \(\int\tau_{\nu_Q}\,d\nu_Q\geq 2^{-k-1}\). The same accepted fact proves the squared loss under domination by \(\nu_Q\). We will also use its elementary domination argument for any two probability measures in the same ambient space. If \(\sigma\geq p\eta\) as measures, with \(p>0\), then

\[
\tau_\sigma(x)\geq p\tau_\eta(x),\qquad
\int\tau_\sigma\,d\sigma
\geq p\int\tau_\eta\,d\sigma
\geq p^2\int\tau_\eta\,d\eta.
\tag{1}
\]

This follows by taking infima of the halfspace inequalities and then integrating a nonnegative function. We apply (1) only where the displayed integrals are defined.

First suppose \(\mu\) is the compact log-affine law in the first assertion. Its density on \(\mathbb R^k\) is log-concave, including the zero extension outside \(K\). Theorem 2.3 of Fradelizi, Madiman and Wang, stated precisely under EXTERNAL SOURCES, gives \(\operatorname{Var}_\mu(\ell(X))\leq k\). Its applicability does not require \(K\) to be smooth or the potential to be strictly convex. Here all moments of \(\ell(X)\) are finite because \(K\) is compact.

Translation preserves halfspaces and their probabilities, while subtracting a constant from \(\ell\) leaves the normalized law unchanged. More explicitly, with \(x_0=\mathbb E_\mu X\), replace \(K\) by \(K-x_0\) and the potential by \(x\mapsto\ell(x+x_0)-\ell(x_0)\). After this replacement, denote the translated law and potential again by \(\mu\) and \(\ell\). We have \(\ell(x)=a\cdot x\) for some \(a\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\mathbb E_\mu\ell(X)=0\), and \(\mathbb E_\mu\ell(X)^2\leq k\). This also covers a constant original potential, for which \(a=0\).

Let \(L=K\cap\{x:|\ell(x)|\leq\sqrt{2k}\}\) and \(p=\mu(L)\). Chebyshev's inequality gives \(p\geq 1/2\). The set \(L\) is compact and convex, and its positive \(\mu\)-mass implies positive Lebesgue volume, hence full dimension. Let \(\mu_L=\mu(\,\cdot\mid L)\). The measure inequality \(\mu\geq p\mu_L\) and (1) reduce the problem to the conditional law on \(L\).

Put \(N=k+1\), \(q(x)=1+a\cdot x/N\), and \(T(x)=x/q(x)\) on the open chart \(\{q>0\}\). On \(L\),

\[
\frac{|a\cdot x|}{N}
\leq\frac{\sqrt{2k}}{k+1}
\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}<\frac34.
\tag{2}
\]

The second inequality is equivalent to \(4k\leq(k+1)^2\). Thus the entire conditional support lies strictly in this chart. No transformation is applied to the remaining mass of \(\mu\).

The inverse map is \(T^{-1}(y)=y/(1-a\cdot y/N)\), on \(\{y:1-a\cdot y/N>0\}\), because \(1-a\cdot T(x)/N=1/q(x)\). Both maps are smooth. The rank-one determinant formula gives

\[
\det DT(x)
=q(x)^{-k}\det\left(I-\frac{x a^{\mathsf T}}{Nq(x)}\right)
=q(x)^{-k}\left(1-\frac{a\cdot x}{Nq(x)}\right)
=q(x)^{-N}>0.
\tag{3}
\]

Moreover, \(T\) maps any segment in its chart onto the segment between the images of its endpoints. In fact, for \(x,z\) in the chart and \(0\leq s\leq1\),

\[
T((1-s)x+sz)
=\frac{(1-s)q(x)T(x)+s q(z)T(z)}{(1-s)q(x)+s q(z)}.
\]

The coefficient of \(T(z)\) runs continuously from zero to one. Consequently \(Q=T(L)\) is convex. It is compact, and (3), or the smooth inverse, shows that it has positive volume. Thus \(Q\) is a convex body.

Let \(\sigma=T_*\mu_L\). This conditional law has exactly the same average depth as \(\mu_L\). To check the assertion for closed halfspaces, fix \(x\in L\), put \(y=T(x)\), and restrict to halfspaces with boundary through the specified point, as justified above. Under \(T^{-1}\), the inequality \(b\cdot u\geq c\) becomes

\[
\left(b+\frac{c a}{N}\right)\cdot y'\geq c.
\tag{4}
\]

If \(c=b\cdot x\) and \(b\neq0\), the normal in (4) is nonzero: its vanishing would imply \(c q(x)=0\), then \(c=0\), and then \(b=0\). The transformed boundary contains \(y\). Conversely, a halfspace \(b'\cdot y'\geq c'\) with boundary through \(y\) pulls back to \((b'-c'a/N)\cdot u\geq c'\), again with nonzero normal by the same argument for the inverse chart. Therefore these transformations match the intersections of all relevant halfspaces with the two supports, and their probabilities agree. It follows that \(\tau_{\mu_L}(x)=\tau_\sigma(T(x))\) for every \(x\in L\), and hence their average depths agree.

Write \(Z_L=\int_L e^{-\ell(x)}\,dx\). By (3), an unnormalized density of \(\sigma\) on \(Q\) is

\[
g(y)=e^{-\ell(T^{-1}y)}q(T^{-1}y)^N,
\qquad
\int_Q g(y)\,dy=Z_L.
\tag{5}
\]

If \(t=\ell(T^{-1}y)\) and \(u=t/N\), then \(\log g(y)=-N\bigl(u-\log(1+u)\bigr)\). For \(|u|\leq3/4\),

\[
0\leq u-\log(1+u)\leq2u^2.
\tag{6}
\]

Indeed, for \(u\geq0\), integrate \(s/(1+s)\) from zero to \(u\) and bound it by \(s\). For \(u=-v\leq0\), integrate \(s/(1-s)\) from zero to \(v\leq3/4\) and bound it by \(4s\). Using (2), (6), and \(|t|\leq\sqrt{2k}\), we obtain \(-4\leq-4k/N\leq\log g(y)\leq0\). Thus \(e^{-4}\leq g(y)\leq1\) throughout \(Q\). Equation (5) gives \(Z_L\leq|Q|\), so the normalized transformed measure satisfies \(\sigma\geq e^{-4}\nu_Q\).

The uniform-body comparison from \(7a3ce13723086670\), projective invariance for the conditional law, and (1) now yield

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu
&\geq p^2\int\tau_{\mu_L}\,d\mu_L\\
&=p^2\int\tau_\sigma\,d\sigma\\
&\geq\frac14 e^{-8}\int\tau_{\nu_Q}\,d\nu_Q\\
&\geq\frac14 e^{-8}2^{-k-1}
=\frac{1}{8e^8\,2^k}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

We next prove the general log-concave assertion. Choose a measurable pointwise log-concave representative \(f\) of the density, and put \(\phi(x)=-\log f(x)\) where \(f(x)>0\), with \(\phi(x)=+\infty\) where \(f(x)=0\). The usual finite-valued definition of a log-concave density suffices. If an extended-valued representative were to take the value \(+\infty\) at a point, log-concavity with a positive-measure set where \(0<f<\infty\) would force \(+\infty\) on a positive-measure affine image of that set, contradicting integrability. Thus no such value is needed. The function \(\phi\) is a proper extended-real convex function. No lower semicontinuity assumption will be required.

Consider its epigraph \(E_0=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t\geq\phi(x)\}\). It is a measurable convex set, and Tonelli's theorem gives

\[
\int_{E_0}e^{-t}\,dx\,dt
=\int_{\mathbb R^k}\int_{\phi(x)}^\infty e^{-t}\,dt\,dx
=\int_{\mathbb R^k}f(x)\,dx=1.
\tag{8}
\]

It follows that \(E_0\) has positive \((k+1)\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so it has nonempty interior. Let \(E=\overline{E_0}\). For a full-dimensional convex set, \(\operatorname{int}\overline{E_0}=\operatorname{int}E_0\subset E_0\), and the boundary of its closure has Lebesgue measure zero. Therefore \(E\setminus E_0\subset\partial E\) is null. Closing the epigraph changes neither (8) nor the measure obtained by multiplying its indicator by \(e^{-t}\). This deals with any lack of lower semicontinuity and with arbitrary density values on the support boundary.

Let \(\widehat\mu\) be the probability measure on \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\) with density \(e^{-t}\mathbf1_E(x,t)\). Equation (8) supplies its normalization, and its marginal under \((x,t)\mapsto x\) is exactly \(\mu\), since the epigraph closure changed the measure only on a null set.

For positive integers \(j\), set \(E_j=E\cap[-j,j]^{k+1}\) and \(b_j=\widehat\mu(E_j)\). For all sufficiently large \(j\), \(E_j\) is a compact full-dimensional convex set: \(E\) has an interior ball, which is eventually contained in these boxes. The sets increase to \(E\), so \(b_j\uparrow1\) by (8). The conditional measure \(\widehat\mu_j=\widehat\mu(\,\cdot\mid E_j)\) has the log-affine density \(b_j^{-1}e^{-t}\mathbf1_{E_j}(x,t)\). Apply (7) in the continuous dimension \(k+1\), and then (1) to \(\widehat\mu\geq b_j\widehat\mu_j\), to obtain

\[
\int\tau_{\widehat\mu}\,d\widehat\mu
\geq b_j^2\int\tau_{\widehat\mu_j}\,d\widehat\mu_j
\geq\frac{b_j^2}{8e^8\,2^{k+1}}.
\]

Letting \(j\to\infty\) proves the same lower bound with \(b_j^2\) replaced by one. This passage uses the monotone convergence of the masses and measure domination; it does not presume a continuity property of depth under a weak limit.

Every closed halfspace \(H\subset\mathbb R^k\) containing \(x\) gives a vertical closed halfspace \(H\times\mathbb R\) containing \((x,t)\), of \(\widehat\mu\)-mass \(\mu(H)\). Thus \(\tau_{\widehat\mu}(x,t)\leq\tau_\mu(x)\) for all \((x,t)\). Integrating and using the exact marginal identity gives

\[
\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu
\geq\int\tau_{\widehat\mu}\,d\widehat\mu
\geq\frac{1}{8e^8\,2^{k+1}}
=\frac{1}{16e^8\,2^k},
\]

as asserted. The lift added exactly one continuous coordinate.

For completeness, we justify the stated fine-lattice consequence, returning here to the original \(K,\ell\) from the statement. The inclusion \(P_m\subset mK\), together with \(D_m\subset P_m\), gives \(P_m\cap\mathbb Z^k=D_m\). Since \(K\) contains an open ball, \(mK\) contains a ball of radius tending to infinity; consequently \(D_m\) contains \(k+1\) affinely independent points for every sufficiently large \(m\). The potential \(J\mapsto\ell(J/m)\) is affine, as required by the lattice notation.

Let \(\mu_m\) put mass \(w_J/W_m\) at \(J/m\). The cube approximation in \(7a3ce13723086670\) applies to a general compact convex \(K\) with the following explicit replacement of its boundary estimate. Choose \(R\geq1\) with \(K\subset B(0,R)\), and use half-open grid cubes of side \(1/m\), with \(\varepsilon=\sqrt{k}/(2m)<1\). For a unit-normal halfspace \(H=\{x:v\cdot x\geq s\}\), the symmetric difference between \(K\cap H\) and the union of cubes whose centers lie in \(K\cap H\) is contained, up to null cube boundaries, in

\[
\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial K)\leq\varepsilon\}
\quad\cup\quad
\{x\in B(0,R+1):|v\cdot x-s|\leq\varepsilon\}.
\]

The first volume tends to zero because \(\partial K\) is compact and null. The second volume is at most \(2\varepsilon V_{k-1}(R+1)^{k-1}\), uniformly in \(v,s\), where \(V_{k-1}\) is the volume of the unit ball in \(\mathbb R^{k-1}\) and \(V_0=1\). The weight function \(e^{-\ell}\) is bounded and uniformly continuous on \(B(0,R+1)\). Replacing its value at each selected cube center by its integral over that cube therefore has an error tending to zero uniformly over all such unions. This proves both \(m^{-k}W_m\to Z>0\) and \(\delta_m:=\sup_H|\mu_m(H)-\mu(H)|\to0\).

Taking infima over the halfspaces containing any fixed point gives \(|\tau_{\mu_m}(x)-\tau_\mu(x)|\leq\delta_m\) for every \(x\). The function \(\tau_\mu\) is Lipschitz: shifting a unit-normal halfspace boundary by \(h\) changes its \(\mu\)-mass by at most \(M V_{k-1}R^{k-1}|h|\), where \(M\) bounds the density of \(\mu\); the same bound holds for the infimum defining depth. The ordinary grid Riemann sums for the continuous function \(e^{-\ell}\tau_\mu\) over \(K\) now give \(\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu_m\to\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu\). Together with the bound by \(\delta_m\), this proves \(\int\tau_{\mu_m}\,d\mu_m\to\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu\). Dilation preserves halfspaces, so \(\tau_{\mu_m}(J/m)=\tau_w(J)/W_m\), proving the claimed limit for \(A_m/W_m^2\). Taking its error smaller than \(1/(16e^8\,2^k)\) proves the stated threshold, with its allowed dependence on \(k,K,\ell\).

Finally, the continuous variance input cannot be applied to arbitrary coarse complete-lattice laws. For \(k\geq2\), take the full-dimensional polytope

\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:0\leq x_1\leq1,
\ 0\leq x_i\leq x_1\text{ for }2\leq i\leq k\},
\qquad
\ell(x)=(k-1)(\log2)x_1.
\]

Its complete lattice support is \(D=P\cap\mathbb Z^k=\{0\}\cup(\{1\}\times\{0,1\}^{k-1})\). Under the weights \(w_J=e^{-\ell(J)}\), the origin has weight one and each of the \(2^{k-1}\) other points has weight \(2^{-(k-1)}\), so \(W=2\). The potential under the normalized atomic law takes the values zero and \((k-1)\log2\), each with probability \(1/2\). Its variance is therefore \((k-1)^2(\log2)^2/4\), which grows quadratically and exceeds \(k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).

This failure of the variance bound does not make the example a shallow-average counterexample. Every support point is isolated by a closed halfspace containing it. The origin is isolated by \(x_1\leq0\). A point \((1,\epsilon_2,\ldots,\epsilon_k)\) uniquely maximizes \(x_1+\sum_{i=2}^k(2\epsilon_i-1)x_i\) over \(D\), so its maximizing halfspace isolates it. Hence \(\tau_w(J)=w_J\) at each support point, and in the unnormalized notation \(A=\sum_{J\in D}w_J\tau_w(J)\) one has \(A/W^2=(1+2^{-(k-1)})/4\geq1/4\). Thus the exact coarse-lattice obstruction here is to transferring the continuous energy-variance mechanism, not a disproof of the desired lattice average bound.
statement:
Let \(k\geq 1\) be a continuous ambient dimension. It is distinct from the integer dimension \(n\) in the locked problem. For a probability measure \(\sigma\) on a Euclidean space, write \(\tau_\sigma(x)=\inf_{H\ni x}\sigma(H)\), with the infimum over closed halfspaces. This is exactly the normalized depth notation of accepted fact \(7a3ce13723086670\); its continuous dimension \(n\) is denoted by \(k\) here.

For every compact full-dimensional convex set \(K\subset\mathbb R^k\), every affine function \(\ell:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R\), and the probability measure \(\mu\) with density \(Z^{-1}e^{-\ell(x)}\mathbf 1_K(x)\), where \(Z=\int_K e^{-\ell(x)}\,dx\), one has

\[
\int_K\tau_\mu(x)\,d\mu(x)
\geq \frac{1}{8e^8\,2^k}.
\]

For every probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^k\) admitting a measurable log-concave Lebesgue density \(f\), one has

\[
\int_{\mathbb R^k}\tau_\mu(x)\,d\mu(x)
\geq \frac{1}{16e^8\,2^k}.
\]

No bounded-support, smoothness, or strict-positivity assumption is imposed on this second density. A density is understood up to Lebesgue-null sets, and a pointwise log-concave representative is used when forming its epigraph.

There is also the following fine-lattice consequence of the first assertion. Fix \(k,K,\ell\) as above. For positive integers \(m\), put \(D_m=mK\cap\mathbb Z^k\), \(P_m=\operatorname{conv}(D_m)\), and \(w_J=e^{-\ell(J/m)}\) for \(J\in D_m\). For all sufficiently large \(m\), these are full-dimensional complete-lattice supports: \(D_m=P_m\cap\mathbb Z^k\). Use the same unnormalized lattice notation as in \(7a3ce13723086670\):

\[
W_m=\sum_{J\in D_m}w_J,\qquad
\tau_w(J)=\inf_{H\ni J}\sum_{I\in D_m\cap H}w_I,\qquad
A_m=\sum_{J\in D_m}w_J\tau_w(J).
\]

Then \(A_m/W_m^2\to\int\tau_\mu\,d\mu\). In particular, there is a threshold \(m_0(k,K,\ell)\) such that \(2^kA_m/W_m^2\geq 1/(16e^8)\) whenever \(m\geq m_0(k,K,\ell)\). The threshold is allowed to depend on all three fixed inputs; no uniform mesh threshold or coarse-lattice bound is asserted.
